utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His microphone is on. Only one, at least. So if you could repeat, Mr. Oric, please, because the interpreters couldn't hear what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can indeed follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. So appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. And also good afternoon to my learned friends of the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel Ms. Patricia Sellers, Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I represent Mr. Oric. We are joined by our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you, too. So any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just a very brief point that I'd like to make and then my colleague would like to make a point as well. Your Honours, we've submitted a list of witnesses and the timetable from those witnesses, and I'd like to inform you that we no longer wish to call Dr. Ilijaz Pilav, for two reasons. First of all, for the fact that his testimony has been rescheduled, he now cannot appear here because he has previous engagements. And secondly, we've assessed the situation very clearly and we've reached the conclusion that his testimony, at least quite a few parts of his testimony, would amount to a repetition and that's why we'd like to withdraw that witness. However, we don't think we'll be wasting any time because this witness that we planned for three days is certainly going to take longer; at least four days, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and we certainly appreciate your appreciating the need to avoid repetition as we go along. I think that would be extremely helpful. Yes, the other two things is -- are the following: Number one, I just wanted to check that you have been served with a copy of the Registrar's response on -- following our decision on your motion to enable document examination and that you are aware of the arrangements that are in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number one. Number two is this: On the 17th of November, those of us that have been here for four years and have been re-elected begin the second term, and then there are -- is two new Judges, one of whom has already taken up her position as permanent Judge as of recently, I mean a few days ago. The other one will be sworn in on the 17th of November. On the 17th of November we have a special ceremony in the morning to be then followed by an Extraordinary Plenary of the Judges. Now, we are supposed -- we are scheduled to sit that day in the morning. The latest I have heard is that at 9.00 there will be this ceremony, swearing-in ceremony and renewal of the term for us, the others, and then immediately after we have this Plenary, which is going to last some time. I mean, it's -- I don't think that it will last all morning. So as we go along I will come back to you more or less with some indication on whether on that particular day we will sit part of the day or whether, if it is possible, we can also possibly shift it to the afternoon. And that's in order not to disrupt your schedule and the testimony that would probably be ongoing at the time. However, between the 7th and the 11th we have spoken amongst ourselves, talked amongst ourselves, and we've come to the conclusion that we need a week to do some very serious housekeeping, to take stock of the evidence that has accumulated since you started the Defence, so that we start placing it in the proper pigeonhole and also have meetings with our staff. And therefore, we propose not to sit between the 7th and the 11th of November. I understand that this is okay with both of you, but I just wanted to confirm -- we've discussed it at length, we've discussed other possibilities, but I think there is no way that we can do work seriously unless we really stop the sittings for -- for a week, also because we can't unduly expect too much from -- or much more from our staff who are working Saturdays and Sundays, included, like most of us. So that's the position, all right? Okay. Thank you. So this week we are going to have practically this one witness we are going to start today. No problems with him, I take it, no health problems or anything of the sort, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honours. Prior to that, I'd like to make another point. We've announced another preliminary issue as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I did want to notify the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution that -- that today we're filing a Rule 68 motion, another motion regarding Rule 68. But it's -- I mention it now because it's marked as urgent and it's -- it truly is urgent for reasons which I'll explain briefly now. I'm afraid I don't have courtesy copies now of the motion because it was completed shortly before we came to Court, but I understand by the first break we'll have courtesy copies. It concerns an article which we've notified on the exhibit list. The ERN, for the record, is 01297984 to 01297987, and in a moment I can distribute that if need be. In essence it is an article entitled "Dogs of War: Slobodan Misic TOP, How I killed Croats and Muslims." In that article, a volunteer from Serbia, Slobodan Misic, who served in Fakovici during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, confesses in a lot of gory detail about how he and others in Serb units in Bratunac, the precise area which we're concerned with with this witness in this case, how he was deployed there by the Serbian Territorial Defence and how he himself killed some 80 -- 70 to 80 people and how, in his estimate, 4.000 to 5.000 Muslims were killed in villages in the area, Zanjevo, Tegare, places which we're very familiar with in this case. He describes killing and decapitating Muslim prisoners. He describes how he and his co-fighters ambushed and killed Muslim villagers who were going in search of food, precisely issues which we've been putting forward since the start of this case, and he tells how he himself even killed Muslim women. When he's asked in the article whether he fought against the Muslim army, he replied: "No, they were civilians, villagers, in most cases insufficiently armed with double-barrelled guns and similar rifles." Exactly the sort of thing that we've been saying since the start of this case. Now that's our theory of the case. The Prosecution, as you know, has been advancing and continues to advance a case according to which, in places like Fakovici, there were nothing but village guards minding their business, tending to their farms, posing no threat to anybody. A completely different picture of events from what's described in this article. And then plainly, therefore plainly, this is exculpatory material; it supports our case, it completely contradicts the picture which they've been seeking to paint of the situation in these Serb villages. And in our motion I've quoted at length Mr. Di Fazio at the Rule 92 bis hearing - I won't go into it now - but talking about village guards as community creations and how these people would simply guard their village at night and watch their farms by day. I personally find it extraordinary that the Prosecution still advances this vision, this picture of events, but there it is, they do. And as long as they do, they absolutely have to disclose to us material which so directly contradicts that case. Now, it's not simply that this article is ERNed - we've found it on the EDS system using Fakovici as a search term - but moreover, we have another document in which a spokesman of the Prosecutor back in November 1997, nearly eight years ago, said that they were aware of Slobodan Misic case, that they were requesting more information from the authorities. And this comes to the crux really: Firstly, our general complaint that why on earth has this not been disclosed to us before now? But secondly, and this is the urgency, is that if the Prosecution does have any further material relating to Slobodan Misic, who, I might add, appears, his name appears in a document I intend to use as an exhibit with this witness, hen we're up to our last Fakovici witness, all the Prosecution Fakovici witnesses who also picture painted this picture of village guards and Serbs peacefully minding their business, they've all gone. We've lost the opportunity to cross-examine them with this material in hand. So if, as it appears from this other document, which I'll hand them up once I've finished these submissions, but in which the spokesperson of the Prosecution said that he would contact the competent bodies of the FRY in order to obtain additional information. If they have any additional information about Slobodan Misic and what he was doing in Fakovici and that area, then we absolutely have to have it before this witness even leaves The Hague so we can still use the evidence with him, albeit without the benefit of proofing him with that material in hand. We've been asking for material on Fakovici since 28th of August, 2003, and we're enclosing in our motion the correspondence. We've referred to the Fakovici units, to any evidence of massacres of Muslims in these areas covered by the indictment. So not only have we been asking for it for nearly two years, it's known to the Prosecution for nearly eight years. Frankly, that is our complaint, that's what our motion deals with. And we would ask the Prosecution and Your Honours to seriously review and urgently review this motion when it's filed this afternoon and take the appropriate steps. And if it would assist Your Honours, I can pass up the exhibits now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can have the exhibits and we will have the courtesy copy after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the Prosecution have advance notice of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I've finished this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is just news --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is news to them like it is to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. That's why we completed the motion really some minutes before we came to Court and so that's why I wanted to mention it now. Obviously, the Prosecution doesn't need to respond immediately unless they wish to, and we'll have the courtesy copies later and we'll ask you to consider it. This is the second document in which the spokesperson of the OTP refers to the Slobodan Misic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll check on this later. I don't think it's the case of you standing up and making any statements at this point, because I don't even know if you know which documents we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. But we will get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. You will have to. I mean, there's no point in discussing that, because if there's going to be a motion, you will need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, but we are taken by surprise as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Wubben. I told you straight away that you're not expected to make any statements now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thought at the time, Your Honour, that it's best to just explain once to Your Honours and to the Prosecution rather than entering into a discussion with the Prosecution minutes before we --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Of course not, no. All right. So this stays here for the time being. Incidentally, while we are on the subject of Rule 68 disclosure, last week there was one incident regarding Rule 66(B) disclosure and there was lack of agreement between you as to whether the relative document had been disclosed in CD format when Mr. Wubben stated that it -- or maintained that it had been disclosed. And you promised to check, Madam Vidovic. I'm asking you so that we complete this -- that particular chapter, at least, and close it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I had already confirmed it on that very day. It was indeed on a CD but that CD included an enormous amount of other documentation, and that was a handwritten document. And we don't seem to be able to find it now, and we have tried a number of search criteria. And this is something that I've already mentioned on a number of occasions when talking to the colleagues from the Prosecution. That is to say, as handwritten documents go, they are simply not recognised by the computer. Even though these documents come under Rule 68 and 66 ter, they simply need to submit them to us, because we've got some CDs with as many as 10.000 different files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see the technician -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I ask Your Honours and the Prosecution to keep your copies of the document which I distributed, because I plan to use it as an exhibit, and of course having distributed the copies now, I could either ask for exhibit numbers, or when we come to it, I'll just assume that everyone has copies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have another copy when we get the copy of the motion in any case, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Alic. Are you receiving --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing you would have already noticed straight away is that while I am speaking in English, what I am saying is being simultaneously translated to you in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is of extreme importance, paramount importance, because you are a witness here and you need to follow exactly what is happening. At the same time, what you say in your own language will be simultaneously translated to us in English, and to others. So it's important that you speak slowly and speak into the microphone so that the interpreters can follow. If at any time there are problems with interpretation, with the reception, either you're not receiving interpretation at all or the level -- sound level is too high or too low, then please draw our attention straight away so that we will look into it and do what is necessary. Very soon you will be starting with your testimony. You are a Defence witness, that is you have been summoned here by the Defence team for Mr. Oric. And our Rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a statement, a solemn statement, equivalent to an oath in several jurisdictions, tantamount to a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. In other words, that your testimony will be truthful. The text is contained in a piece of paper that Madam Usher is going to hand to you now. Please read it out aloud and -- read that text aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. You are going to be here with us testifying for a few days, Mr. Alic, and the first part of our testimony will be answering -- will consist in answering questions from Mr. Jones, who is co-counsel for Mr. Oric. When the examination-in-chief is finished, then it will be followed by a cross-examination, and it will be Ms. Patricia Sellers, the lady in the middle next to the gentleman, next to the lead counsel, who will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether you will be able to go back home the end of this week or not pretty much depends on you. I can assure you, because I know everyone here, that everyone will do their level best to try and send you back home by the weekend. But if you give lengthy answers, if you beat around the bush, if you give more information than is required from you when you are asked a question, then obviously you are going to be here for longer. So I -- my suggestion to you is that you, when answering questions, irrespective of where they are coming from, Defence and Prosecution, you not only try to answer truthfully and concisely, but you try to restrict your answer to what is being asked from you. If it is a question that requires a simple, straightforward yes or no answer, then give a simple yes or no answer. If, however, you believe that in addition to that it's better if you give some kind of explanation to elucidate, to clarify, your answer, then just ask that you be allowed to explain further and we will certainly let you explain further unless it's the case of obviously not wanting more information. Have I made myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfectly clear, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones will be examining you in chief. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Good afternoon from me, Witness.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, until just -- we will be sitting right through to 7.00 today. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I presume there will be a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. There are going to be two breaks because I've been asked to have two breaks. So there will be a break after an hour and a half, another break after he second session of an hour and a half, and then obviously the last part which will be -- If, however, you notice that your witness is getting tired or you or Madam Vidovic are getting tired, then of course we will stop whenever you tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Your Honour. You had me worried. I thought I was going to have to go right through until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see that we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see Ms. Sellers on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are discussing issues of time and timing. Since we have had a change in some of the presentation of the Defence case, I wonder if the Defence could possibly tell us now how long they intend for their direct examination for this witness to be because it seems that that might have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. How long do you expect -- I suppose from what I could gather from Ms. Vidovic, it's two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So essentially six hours -- six hours is my best estimate now, but possibly a bit more. Over the course of proofing, the estimate did go up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And in that case, what do you anticipate as time requirement on your part?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would state that it would probably be 100 per cent of the time that they've allotted, and if it is either prolonged or reduced we would certainly try and inform not only on the Trial Chamber but also Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So tentatively we're saying two days for Prosecution, two days for Defence for the time being, and then obviously we play it by the ear as it goes along, especially since we are not going to have another witness after this witness later on this week. So we could afford to go to -- no, we can't, because Friday is a UN holiday. So we need to finish by --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I believe it's Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay then. So we can go -- spill onto Friday then. But tentatively, let's say two days Prosecution, two days Defence. All right. And then if we have an emergency or a crisis, then obviously we'll find a remedy. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, please for the record give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Ibro Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you tell us, incidentally, is that a common or uncommon name in your area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It's a common name. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: A bit like John Jones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the Srebrenica-Potocari memorial, you see Alic everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I should have said a popular name because I always ask if -- I say my name is a popular name rather than a common name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you were born on the 1st of January, 1971 in Jagodnja in Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I want to know if you heard anything, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was an interruption in the interpretation process at one point, and that's probably what the witness is referring to. If my colleague could please just repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we have problems here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the interpreters say something so that we can follow from here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: English booth interpretation speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Alic, and sorry, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. To repeat the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you were born on the 1st of January, 1971?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I assume it's not the question, because it's a straightforward one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me start again. Tell us when you were born.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 1971, in Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what municipality is Jagodnja in?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you complete primary school in Fakovici in 1986?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before the war in Bosnia, did you live in Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that a Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in Jagodnja, were there approximately 45 houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is there an adjacent village called Joseva which has approximately 40 houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that was also a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that before the war there were in total about 550 to 600 inhabitants in Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were these villages in the local commune of Zlijebac?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll distribute a new map now in order to locate these places. It's the large map similar to the one we used with another witness before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give it a number straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is going to be Defence Exhibit D8 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D827, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 827, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, I'm going to ask you to do two different things with this map. If you look at the map to your left, I want you -- if you don't have a pen, I can give you one. It's actually, I want you to underline Jagodnja and Joseva and then highlight some other places.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: This is Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with due respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The computer monitor mode is not on. I don't know if any of my colleagues have it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if any of my colleagues -- yes, it's come on now. All right. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So now I'm going to ask if the witness be given a highlighter, or at least a different coloured pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Zlijebac , was that a Serb village before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you circle Zlijebac, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was Fakovici also a nearby village to your village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The distance between Jagodnja and Fakovici was about seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before the war, was Fakovici a Serb, Muslim, or mixed village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was predominantly Serb. There was a small number of Muslims living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So if you could circle Fakovici for us in green as well, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, before the war did you go to Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you and other Muslims from Jagodnja and Joseva go to cafes there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you go to school in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How well would you say you know Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I know Fakovici because I went to school there for four years, elementary school. And every week I would pass through Fakovici on my way back from Bratunac, because that was an important bus stop on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know a place called Zanjevski Potok?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is that part of Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before the war, who lived there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Muslims. We used to call them Jurks [as interpreted] and Gypsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: These were Gypsies who were Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They had Muslim names, but that's what some people called them. I don't think I could venture into that sort of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'm going to ask you on the map to mark the villages in your area which were Serb -- Serb ethnicity before the war. And if you could mark them and then say what you're marking at the same time. The surrounding villages which were Serb before the war.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: We can start from the village of Blazijevici, the village of Godzevici, the village of Klekovici, the village of Caklovici, Bradici, and Jaketici. And then we have Zlijebac, which I have already circled. Down the Drina in the direction of Fakovici one comes across Kutijesi, Boljevici, Radijevici --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could stop there for a moment. For Radijevici you've encircled an area near the Drina. We see the letters Radijevici, or the word Radijevici, further away from the Drina. Do you have any explanation why that is?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: This village of Radijevici is an old village where no Serbs used to be. The Serbs lived in the field next to the river Drina; that's Radijevici. They all lived there and this population was there before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that's the old part of Radijevici up in the hills; is that it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And people -- were people living there at the start of the war in Bosnia, in that old part?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Not according to my information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if you could continue marking in green only the Serb villages which surrounded Jagodnja and Joseva before the war, and you can proceed now from the direction of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I'm going now in the direction of a Muslim village when you go past Radijevici. This village is called Zanjevo, and then you come across Fakovici, which already has a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. So don't mark Abdulici or Zanjevo. If you can move on to Mlecva, was that Serb or Muslim before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That probably suffices for now, thank you. You can leave the map there but turn away from it for the moment. Now, before the war, did your family have a business?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What was that business?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: My family chopped timber. We had a place, a mini factory, where wood was cut, a mini saw works we used to call it. We would cut up timber or whatever was needed. People came and asked for whatever they needed, and we would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did people come from the whole area, then, or just the local area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The whole area or just locally?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Not from Fakovici, but away from Fakovici; Zanjevo, Radijevici, everybody came to see us whenever they needed something, and they would get their wood from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you also own a tractor before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you travel the local area with your tractor, doing business in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the villages you've circled in green and obviously your own villages, would you say you know them well?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, the Judges have indicated to us that we have sufficient evidence on the background of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I'm not going to ask about tensions or anything of that nature. I'm simply going to ask you this: You've told us how you used to go to cafes in Fakovici. Did there come a time when Muslims were no longer welcome in those cafes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: That was in mid-April, between mid-April and May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there still one cafe in Fakovici where you still went?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Who owned that cafe?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The owner was Petko Jovanovic; this is the one that we still went to after we were told that we were no longer welcome in the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to come to the first one in a moment, but Petko Jovanovic, did he do any other good things for you Muslims in that period?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. What?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: He did good things for us whenever we came to his cafe, as we called it. He would give us a warm welcome, he would give us everything that we needed, and upon our return, since the clashes with the Serb side had already started, he would see us out of the cafe and off in our direction back from Fakovici, the road that we took on the way back, because Serbs would meet us along the road, swear at us. They would sing their own Serb songs, that sort of thing. He would see us through all this trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. You say when you were coming back -- the direction back from Fakovici. Where were you -- where were you coming from before then? Is this on the way back from Bratunac that would you would go through Fakovici or simply from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Before, there used to be a bus stop there, and our people who were on their way back from Bratunac would get off there and walk to Jelena. Sometimes we went to the cafe, or sometimes we just walked on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this Petko Jovanovic would protect you from harassment by Serbs; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Petko Jovanovic and his --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that we are very much in a background phase, but just to be careful about some leading. "Did anything happen to Petko Jovanovic?" If it's a question of time, it appears that with this witness we will have ample time. We're just cautious about leading that might not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sellers. Mr. Jones, please note.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll cease leading from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Petko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to what people from Abdulici told me, after the expulsion of those people who then came to our villages, Jagodnja and Joseva, they told us that Petko Jovanovic had been expelled from Fakovici in mid-May and that his house was burnt down at the same time as was his cafe. They told us that Petko Jovanovic was at Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who burnt down his house, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: According to what those people told us, only the Serbs from Fakovici could have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, do you know Slavko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What did you know about him before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: While I was still a student at the Fakovici school, Slavko Jovanovic worked at the school as security, and he worked in the boiler room. He was president of the SDS in Fakovici, and he was in fact one of the organisers of the local branch of the SDS. He encouraged Serb soldiers to be nationalistic and to drive Muslims out of Abdulici and the other Muslim villages in the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In early 1992, did you ever see him in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What sort of uniform?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Olive-drab, the one they used in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever see him with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I didn't myself, but people from Abdulici did see him carrying a weapon. When he came to the village in early May, he would come carrying a pistol and automatic rifle slung around his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he own a cafe in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What was that cafe called?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Medena.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned how you were only welcome in one cafe, that of Petko Jovanovic. Were you welcome in the cafe owned by Slavko Jovanovic, as a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No. As early as the beginning of April, we were no longer welcome there. Whenever we entered that particular cafe, we were taken aback by what we saw there. There were photographs of Slobodan Milosevic there, caps with kokardas hung along the walls - it's a Serb symbol. It was very difficult to get proper service if you were a Muslim in that cafe. There was nobody to wait on you, and after a while we realised that we were no longer welcome there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in Fakovici itself before the war, before the war started, did you see any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: On one occasion I was going from Bratunac -- it was in mid-March, and I was going from the bus station at Bratunac accompanied by two or three friends. And as we came out of the station, we crossed the bridge and turned in the direction of the school, and we should have turned by a creek going to Jagodnja. And in front of the old school we found quite a few soldiers wearing their olive-drab uniforms. And they were standing in front of the school. We didn't actually linger because we kind of panicked and continued on our way to Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say -- I think you said "quite a few." How many, approximately, would you estimate?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Between 50 and a hundred. So one could see it quite easily with the naked eye; that was our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were they doing in front of the old school?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: At that moment when we came along, they were simply standing there. As to what they did next, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything from anyone about what -- what, if any, military activity was going on in Fakovici in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In the beginning we heard from people from Zanjevo who used to come to Jagodnja and Joseva. And we heard from them that they had some kind of exercises in Fakovici and that they had shooting exercises above Grabovacka Rijeka. It is a creek in fact, called Ruljevici, I believe. It was just above Grabovacka Rijeka itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've told us how at a certain time you weren't welcome -- you Muslims weren't welcome in cafes in Fakovici. Did there come a time when Muslims couldn't safely go to Fakovici at all?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was later. By the end of April, nobody dared go down from Jagodnja and Joseva to Fakovici. After the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But once you could no longer go into Fakovici, could you still see what was going on in the village from where you were?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We could see and some people did go in that direction, and they could observe what went on there. I did not go myself, but it was also confirmed from people from Abdulici, that is to say the events that went on in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can show us on the map what the closest was that someone from Jagodnja and Joseva could get to Fakovici, where these people went who were looking into the village, if there's some spot that you can mark.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a slope above Fakovici. It is a hilly area, and you can only walk there. It is inaccessible to any vehicles and it was called stijena, "rocks," 2 or 300 metres, and you could go there and you had a full view of all of Fakovici. And that was on the way to school, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say 2 or 300 metres --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, this is where it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you make it larger?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, because that's barely visible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, the witness puts a cross on the map at 35 minutes of Fakovici. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you say "2 to 300 metres," what distance are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You said that this location, rocks, "stijena," was 2 or 300 metres. 2 or 300 metres from where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... or what, because I saw one of the guards assisting him with the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Ah, yes -- can you see -- I won't ask my client a direct question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, there was a problem with the other microphone once again. One of the mikes is not working. I can only see the transcript, but I can't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I think -- Usher, see if you can assist. If you can't, then we get a technician. I'm sorry to have interrupted you like this, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I saw him getting a little bit agitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, it's important for him to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it's working now. Is it all right now, Usher? No? So we need a technician. Do you want to stop, Mr. Jones, until it's fixed, or shall we proceed? It's working now, I think. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, everything's fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. This site which you've described, it was 2 or 300 metres from where?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: From Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've described how people would look from there into Fakovici. Was that only with the naked eye or did they have binoculars or any other visual aid?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It could be seen with the naked eye, but they did have hunting binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there another spot near Jagodnja and Joseva where people could look and see what was happening in Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a place called Mackovac. It's just above Zanjevo. Yeah, above Zanjevo. And Zanjevo Polje and Radovica Potok and part of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Fakovici could be seen from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could you also please mark that location on the map, perhaps with a Y to distinguish from the previous X.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we have another X, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, no, it's not fine. Could you put a circle around that X, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just for the record, the witness put an encircled X to show Zanjevo Polje between -- halfway between Fakovici and Joseva, between Fakovici and Joseva. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us how you had conversations with people from Abdulici on various matters.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you speak to them about what was happening in Fakovici in April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were they telling you about what was going on in -- first of all, in their villages, in Zanjevo and Abdulici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: They used to tell us that Serbs from Fakovici would come and give them an ultimatum to surrender and leave their villages, and they took their weapons off them. And it was at around the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did there come a time when the Muslims in Zanjevo and Abdulici in fact left their villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know why they left their villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Those people had to leave because they were no longer desirable in that part of Fakovici because they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How about Tegare and Orlica. Are you familiar with those places?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we're all familiar with those places and we had heard that they, too, had been driven out of their homes between the 1st and the 15th of May. And some people had arrived at Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we probably don't need to go into this in great detail, but did they leave of their own volition or were they forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: They were forced to leave by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was there a time when in fact Zanjevo and Abdulici were burned, or the houses there were burned?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was up until mid-May 1992. Until mid-May 1992 none of the Muslims ever went to Abdulici or Zanjevo because basically all Muslims had been driven away, and they arrived to Jagodnja and Joseva and others went to other places. And there were too many civilians. It was almost impossible to count them all, and nobody was able to have a full overview of where they went, in what direction, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the burning of these houses in Abdulici and Zanjevo, was that something that you in Jagodnja and Joseva could actually see yourselves?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It wasn't possible to see from Jagodnja and Joseva because we were on the other side of the hill. It was a hilly area, and from Jagodnja and Joseva you had no visibility, as it were, because we had to go to that place I marked on the map, Mackovac, and from there you could see the fires. And as to these refugees who came from the village of Zanjevo, they told us that the houses had been set on fire, that everything was taken from them, that they were driven out, and that some civilians had been captured and taken in the direction of Fakovici. And they came exhausted, with some torn clothes on their backs, basically, and that was all. And they came during the night, and it was difficult to even imagine what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just finally on the -- on whether or not one could see -- sorry, my microphone seems to have switched off. All sorts of technical problems today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder -- it doesn't -- okay. I'm not hearing it in my headphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are hearing you, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The burning of houses in Abdulici and Zanjevo, would that have been visible in Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Would you say that anyone in Fakovici would be able to see that burning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Of course an objection to this type of hypothetical question; anyone, depending on where they're positioned in Fakovici. I understand Your Honours' position on that, but we would like to state that for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I'm happy with the previous answer he's given, that it would have been visible in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's enough, because obviously it depends on who the subject matter would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Subject, rather than subject matter, would be, and where he or she happens to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that it's visible in Fakovici is sufficient for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you receive -- you've mentioned refugees arriving in Jagodnja and Joseva from Zanjevo and Abdulici. Did you later receive refugees from other areas?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you name some of the places where you received refugees from, and this is - to have a time frame - in the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning of May, the refugees from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He -- as I understand, the witness has a problem. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay now. There was just some background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at any rate, the refugees from a place called Skelani who had been driven out of their houses, and some also came from Dobraki, from Resagici, from Tihici, from Daljegosta. All those refugees came in towards Jagodnja and Joseva and mostly at night. They could only move at night, basically, through forests and they were just carrying some handbags and nothing else. They didn't even manage to bring food. And so we had to accept all those refugees in Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you also receive refugees from Tegare or Orlica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Two or three refugees from Tegare arrived because they had some relatives there, and they stayed for a very short time and then they went somewhere else, I don't know where. And so those places were emptied as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when there was Serb patrols around Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Those Serb patrols could be seen already in the first half of April in Ravni Hrg, around Jagodnja, because Jagodnja and Joseva are surrounded by forest, basically, on all sides. And they were seen at the lake above Jagodnja -- or rather, it's a place we used to call lake. It's a village called Jezero. And those patrols could be seen there on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were the people wearing who were participating in this patrol -- in these patrols?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those people wore uniforms. They wore military uniforms and they had automatic weapons. Yeah, they had automatic weapons. They were the real Serb soldiers; that's what we called them, Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know where they were coming from, from which area or which villages they were coming from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Jezero above Jagodnja and Joseva, as I've explained earlier. They came from the direction of Fakovici, and on the other side they were coming from Skelani and the other Serb villages I've mentioned before; Klekovici and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you have a relative called Mustafa Alic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he encounter one of these patrols?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the middle of April, he went towards Fakovici because he had a hunting rifle, and he had a license for that hunting rifle - he was a hunter, by the way - and at Mackovac he was stopped by Serb soldiers, and they asked him, Why are you going down this road? And he said he wanted to go hunting, but his hunting rifle was taken off him and he was told that it was the Crisis Staff at Fakovici that issued the order on the basis of which Muslims were not around -- allowed to walk around the nearby woods armed. And they said to him that in order to receive a certificate for that rifle he had to contact the Crisis Staff at Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned these two places from which you could -- or people from Jagodnja and Joseva could see into Fakovici or part of Fakovici. Was it possible to see the road, Bratunac-Skelani road, from those positions?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In early 1992, did you see or did you hear of people seeing military vehicles on the road going through Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard from people that they had seen military vehicles driving towards Fakovici; trucks and transport vehicles or whatever. Military vehicles, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, were you aware, aside from vehicles, of helicopters flying in your area in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I myself saw a helicopter which came from the area of Jezero and Skelani, and in the valley of Jagodnja, that is to say just below Jagodnja and Joseva, there was a river called Jagodnja and the helicopter was flying in that area towards Fakovici. I saw it at Jagodnja as it flew by.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was approximately at the end of March, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know whether this helicopter was being operated by Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: By Serbs, because Muslims could not have flown that helicopter, according to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, if you could cover it now, it would avoid us putting a question later on, if it did have any markings or distinguishing marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alic, you heard the question. Were there any markings on this helicopter that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You didn't see any markings?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you either -- did you hear from other people or gather any information as to what these helicopters were doing, flying around in this area?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I believe he's testified having seen a helicopter, so I don't know now whether we're talking about helicopters or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're right, Ms. Sellers. Please rephrase your question, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Aside from the helicopter you saw, did you hear about whether there were other helicopters flying in your area in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any others, but I did hear about them flying over other areas and around these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: People from Zanjevo told us that a helicopter landed in Fakovici and they said that it was in order to unload some weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you about some specific individuals. Do you know Ognjen Markovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Bato.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where is he from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: From Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did he come to Jagodnja and Joseva at any time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: At some point in mid-April, the first fortnight in April, at any rate, he came to Jagodnja together with an armed and uniformed policeman who was called Dane, and I can't remember his family name. And there were two other people with them. And they came to my sawmill. And we were told we were not allowed to go into the forests and that he had been appointed as some kind of technical manager or a ranger, rather, and that we were not allowed to go into the woods or cut any wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When he said "you," was he just referring to your family, the family Alic, or something else?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: He meant all Muslims, that they had no business going into the woods. But he came to our place because many Muslims would gather around this sawmill, and so he first drew our attention to this fact and then he turned to the others and said that they had no business going into the woods either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know then or suspect what the real reason was or what the main reason was why Muslims were not being allowed to go into the woods?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The real reason, as we concluded was -- well, because we had seen Serbs on patrol in the area, we concluded that the forests were full of Serb soldiers, and that was in order to avoid any inconvenient conflicts at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Did Ognjen Markovic come back to Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came back after a week or ten days. And he asked for all weapons to be surrendered, because there were reserve police officers in our village, and he said that all rifles had to be relinquished to the Crisis Staff in Fakovici and that that applied to hunting rifles as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did he -- did he come alone or did he come with others?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: He came alone with a police officer called Stevan, as he had the last time around, with two other people from Fakovici or from Skelani. They said they belonged to the Skelani municipality and that we were part of the municipality, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one correction. What the transcript reflects is the witness saying that he had come with a police officer from Skelani and not a police officer called Stevan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said Stevan to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Do you confirm that, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you confirm what Ms. Vidovic has just pointed out, that you never said that you came with a police officer called Stevan, but that you had come with a police officer from Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's not him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From Skelani. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that Ognjen Markovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just clarify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish what you need to finish and then we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that Ognjen Markovic came to Jagodnja and Joseva with a police officer from Skelani; that's your evidence?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we can have a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It will be a 25-minute break, starting from now. That means we will approximately -- start again at 10 minutes or 12 minutes past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, before you proceed, the motion, or I think what is a courtesy copy of the motion is with us. All right. Since this is still a courtesy copy and I don't know if it has been already served on the Prosecution or not, obviously I cannot grab the Prosecution and say, respond today, but you would be required to respond tomorrow, first thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To confirm, we have received the courtesy copy, but we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. But obviously you'll need to check your things. So first thing tomorrow we start precisely with this. And if necessary, there will be an oral exchange of arguments and then we'll see what our position will be on the matter. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour. I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One thing, Your Honour: I was informed during the break that the witness might be concerned that he's going to be here for a longer period than anticipated. I'm not -- I'm not sure -- obviously we're not communicating with the witness, but I just thought I'd say in open Court that by the end of today, certainly by the middle of the day tomorrow I'll have a better idea of how long I'll be and there might be another indication of how long he'll be here in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. And I think the witness heard me say earlier on today that we'll make an effort -- everyone will make an effort to make sure that he's back home by the weekend. He needs to cooperate, too, and so far I think he has cooperated fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And I'm sure we can make progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic before the break, you said now Ognjen Markovic, Bato, came to Jagodnja and Jaseva with a reserve police from Skelani, and they said that you too were now in Skelani. Now, my question is: Up until then, your villages were in Bratunac municipality, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, I see Ms. Vidovic standing. What's your -- microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It's the interpretation again. I don't think my colleague actually said that Ognjen Markovic was a reserve police officer in Skelani but rather that he came with a reserve police officer from Skelani. These are material matters and therefore we insist that the transcript be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I think I heard that, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. So let's proceed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can repeat your question just for formality's sake and practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Before the break you said that Ognjen Markovic, Bato, came to Jagodnja with a reserve police officer from Skelani and that they said that they belonged to Skelani municipality and that you now did, too. My question was: Until then, certainly Jagodnja and Joseva were in Bratunac municipality, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know what this was about, this idea that your village was now in a new municipality?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: According to Bato Markovic's explanation, these villages were now part of the newly founded municipality of Skelani. And Jagodnja and Joseva, too, were part of Skelani municipality. He said all the way from Bjelovac and down the river Drina and all the way down as far as Skelani, all that now belonged to Skelani municipality and so did we.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. And you also said how these men said that the reserve policemen in Jagodnja and Joseva had to hand in their weapons to the Crisis Staff in Fakovici. Did they do so?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you in Jagodnja and Joseva keep any weapons of any description?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: We only kept our hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how many rifles, roughly, in Jagodnja and in Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: There were two in Jagodnja and four in Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a new exhibit which we'd like to pass out at this stage with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usher has just left the room, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. The assistance of the registry. And for the record, the ERN is 03609354 to 03609355. It's a document headed "Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior Serbian Municipality of Skelani, Skelani Public Security Station." And the date is 18 September 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, you'll see a list of names here and you'll see that they were all activated into the Skelani reserve police force on 1 April, 1992. And then if you turn to page 2, both B/C/S and English, we see the heading "Branch station in Fakovici," and then there is a list of six names of people who were transferred from the Skelani reserve police force to the Fakovici branch station on 1 April 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as we saw, this document refers to the Serbian municipality of Skelani. The Serbian municipality. Does that fit with what you were telling us now about Serbs from Fakovici saying that they belonged to Skelani municipality and that you did, too?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And even before the war, was there a link --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. Even before the war - this is dated September 1992 - but before the war was the -- were there links between Fakovici and Skelani?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in this document we see it's the Skelani public security station and there's a Fakovici -- there's a Fakovici branch office -- branch station, sorry. And as I pointed out the date, 1st of April, 1992, that's obviously before the war, you see that there were people --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, and we know that in the middle of Fakovici there was a police checkpoint as early as April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And who is it who set up that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The checkpoint was set up by Skelani municipality, the one in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd just ask for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, Mr. Jones. This document, which consists of two pages in the Serbo-Croat version and three pages in the English version, the ERN being 03609354 to 355 is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D828.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, just to see how the situation developed from this point on, in Jagodnja and Joseva you've surrendered all but a handful of hunting rifles. You've told us that at this time it was no longer safe for Muslims to go to Fakovici. You're surrounded, as we've seen --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As we've seen on the map, your village was surrounded by Serb villages --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I would really think that that might be a mischaracterisation. I've seen that the witness has pointed out some Serb villages. He's not testified as anything being surrounded and that's not what I see from his geographical marking. If counsel would like to pose some questions and if we want to make that a bit clearer, I would just ask that he not be misleaded [sic] on that if that's not his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You are right in toto, yeah, I think this can be so, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can do it with the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- on the other hand, when the witness was asked in the beginning to mark the Serb villages, I remember Mr. Jones telling the witness very clearly the Serb villages around Jagodnja and the other, Joseva --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it is a mischaracterisation and it isn't at the same time. So it's -- but I think there's no harm in raising the matter. I don't really think I can consider it as an objection in its own right, but I think it's in the interest of Mr. Jones himself to address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, I certainly will address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you look at the map, Mr. Alic, you've circled on that map the Serb villages which were, if not surrounding, which were in the vicinity of Jagodnja and Joseva. You've pointed out two villages, Zanjevo and Abdulici, which were Muslim villages. You also told us that those -- Muslims left those villages.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So when did they leave the villages of Abdulici and Zanjevo, roughly?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In the first half of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So taking it from that period, after Muslims had left Zanjevo and Abdulici, and looking at the map, isn't it right that Jagodnja and Joseva had on certainly three sides only Serb villages? And I'll specific them: Mlecva, Fakovici, Radijevici, Boljevici, Kutijesi, Zlijebac, Jaketici, Bradici, Caklovici, Godzevici, Klekovici and Blazijevici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may explain. By your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jagodnja and Joseva are surrounded on all sides, including the road leaving Jagodnja and Joseva, with just woodlands around the two villages. And the distance to the first Muslim village is about 10 kilometres. I said at the outset that in the forests around Hrg, Ravni Hrg, Serb patrols had been observed moving about. So to all practical intents, both villages were entirely surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've also told us how all but a few hunting rifles were handed in to the Serbs. Now, my question is: Following that --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Following that, did the Serbs leave you in peace or how did things develop?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
