utterances.text: They didn't leave us in peace for a second. Early May, even as early as late April, there was shooting from the Ravni Hrg area. A farmer, or rather a shepherd who was there watching the sheep, was wounded. That was in late April, or sometime between mid-April and late April, he was seriously wounded in his leg, and this was done by Serbs patrolling the area. They fired at this shepherd of ours and they kept firing away around the woods all the way through the night, using a wide variety of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. What sort of weapons? If you can name a couple of those weapons for us.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: They had automatic weapons, automatic rifles, M-48, the old kind with a long range, could be used to hit targets as far away as 1.200 metres; they had machine-guns and automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were these hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does the term "village guards" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It's called village guards and we know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And were these weapons that the Serbs were using to shoot into your village, were they the sorts of weapons that village guards would have?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution may suggest that the Serbs were shooting into your village even though you'd disarmed, for all intents and purposes, because they were afraid of Muslims, because they were frightened of you. Is that a realistic suggestion?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Would you care to elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: There would have been no reason for the Serbs to be afraid of us. We remained in those two villages and we had no intention of offending anyone, let alone harming or, in the worst of cases, killing anyone. There was panic among us. If it had been our intention to do anything like that, we would not have surrounded [as interpreted] our weapons to begin with when the police came over and asked for it. We wouldn't have done anything like that. We would have resisted their arrival when they first came to ask for us to hand over our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And for the transcript, I think it's "surrendered our weapons" rather than "surrounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So why were they attacking, the Serbs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: What we believed, or rather, what I believed at the time, the Serbs attacked us in such a way as to expel us, as they had done elsewhere earlier on. We were also told by the Serbs who had threatened us that we were to leave Jagodnja and Joseva and that we should leave the Drina area, go at least as far as 40 kilometres from the river itself, and that we would no longer be allowed to remain in those areas for the simple fact that we were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who said that to you specifically?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: A neighbour of ours, Vidoje Maksimovic, came to our village and asked us to surrender so that we might be escorted out of the area. Our people asked for some sort of guarantee, whether they could guarantee our security on the way out, and he said that he could offer no guarantee. The only thing he could guarantee was to get us as far as Zlijebac and Fakovici, but nothing else. He told us explicitly that we were to go as far as 40 kilometres out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did he deliver that message to you that you were to go out 40 kilometres out of the area in his own capacity or was that a message he was delivering on someone else's behalf?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: This is something that he told us on behalf of Skelani municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, 40 kilometres is obviously quite a distance. How far is Srebrenica from the Drina, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The distance must be, in my estimate at least, about 20 or 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So according to what he said, there should be no Muslims in Srebrenica either?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would ask that Defence stop not only suggesting to the witness, because it's obvious just from what the questions the Defence has asked the witness and the answers, that that was not the suggestion. That might be an opinion that's being reached. The only thing I would ask, that the commentary of Defence counsel as to whether 40 kilometres is a long distance or not, the witness might very much agree that it is a long distance, or he might say, no, I look at 100 kilometres as being long. If we would stop having commentary by the Defence witness [sic] on the evidence that's given and allow the witness, Mr. Alic, to please continue his testimony straightforward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Distance and relativity of distance is not that important. But the other one, the other point raised is important. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think Ms. Sellers is slightly overstating it to say that she ask that the commentary stop being given as if I am -- as if this has been some repeated offence on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's one comment which she's free to object to, but let's not have her characterising my examination-in-chief unfairly either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you were right there, too. But this Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The other matter is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Approach in another manner if you want to, or abandon it. It's up to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to understand what the objection was in terms of Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The objection was, as I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is it that it's obvious that all the Muslims would have to leave Srebrenica because it's within 40 kilometres? If that's obvious, then I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but I -- again, I mean, I think you have to put the question in a different manner. I'm trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I just lost it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can revisit it as a matter of pure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You said 40 kilometres is obviously quite a distance. Ms. Sellers objected to that. I don't attach that much importance to that because 40 kilometres is a distance, for someone coming from Malta, like me, it's twice the length of the island, so you can imagine that it is quite a distance. But I don't attach that much importance to that -- to that point --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me approach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then you said: How far is Srebrenica from the Drina? And he said about 20 to 25 kilometres. And then your question was: "So according to what he said, there should be no Muslims in Srebrenica either."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It follows as a matter of pure logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you're drawing the conclusion for him. Maybe the conclusion that he drew at the time was that Srebrenica did not come into it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll put the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because Srebrenica has got separate characteristics and qualities of its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll approach it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I suggest. Because otherwise, it's harmless. We'll still get there, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When Vidoje Maksimovic said on behalf of Skelani municipality that Muslims weren't to live, or had to leave, an area 40 kilometres from the Drina, did you understand or would you understand that to mean Srebrenica, based on its distance from the Drina?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, leaving Srebrenica aside, that would mean, would it not, did you understand it this way, that certainly Muslims living along the Drina in Zanjevo, Abdulici, Tegare, would no longer be allowed by the Serbs to live in their homes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've testified that in fact they were forced to leave their homes by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've told us earlier about how refugees came to Zanjevo, and you mentioned a number of places; Skelani, Dobraki, Tihici, and I think you described how they came at night. Were these just adults or were they just men, women, children; who exactly came?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: As I stated previously, there were whole villages that were being driven out; women, men, and children. That's what happened in early May: People left the area for fear of shooting, for anger, because they had been threatened, because they'd heard the songs that in themselves affected the population in a negative way and made people flee. They would arrive during rainy nights - it was a very rainy spring - people were hungry, people had nothing to wear. They were facing a disaster. It's difficult to describe all of this at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one clarification. You mentioned that they felt threatened because they'd heard songs and because of fear of shooting. Was that all that made them leave their villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serb soldiers would come to the villages. They would drive people out, they would loot. There's nothing they didn't do. They would catch those who were a bit better off. That's what happened in Jagodnja and Joseva. People were literally driven out of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, roughly how many refugees came to Jagodnja and Joseva in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, or rather in May, until as late as mid-May, all the villages had been emptied. All the people had been driven out of those villages. In my estimate, between 500 and 1.000 people passed through my village to the extent that I could notice. There were between 50 and 100 refugees in my house alone, both day and night. I myself had nowhere to sleep. We even used the stables, the cowsheds, and some other outbuildings that we had. We put some people up at the school building, which was still open at the time, and people literally had to be accommodated there. They would spend nights in the open sometimes or would leave and go elsewhere once they had realised that they couldn't all fit there. They'd brought no clothes along, no blankets, no food to have around, simply because they hadn't had the time to bring these things with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was anyone in Jagodnja and Joseva registering these people, registering their names and keeping track of who was arriving?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No, it was just impossible to have a list of all these people because they were coming from Abdulici, Zanjevo, Skelani, a place called Buradji. They had to come through the forest. From all over the place. As they fled their homes, they came to us, and it was simply impossible to keep a proper record of all that, and nobody even attempted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could keep your answers slightly shorter, otherwise we might have difficulty making progress. Now, you've mentioned shooting with various firearms into your village. Did there ever come a time when your village was attacked by artillery?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you explain for us briefly where the artillery was firing from and if you know the calibre of the artillery.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In the first half of May, the village of Joseva was shelled from Fakovici, from Bijeli Kamen, Buradji. And infantry was shooting at us from the surrounding forests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And from Fakovici do you know what artillery was being used?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Mortars. 80- and 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were those mortars in Fakovici, the 80-millimetre and 120-millimetre?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then Bijeli Kamen, what was the calibre of the artillery firing from there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The calibre was 80 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, how do you actually know that artillery was firing from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The refugees were still coming from that direction, and they knew that Joseva and Jagodnja were being shelled, and they told us about it. And as to Bijeli Kamen, we could see it through our binoculars. We could see -- by using binoculars you could see the mortars at Bijeli Kamen , because we did have this improvised binoculars. Actually, they're hunting binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was anyone in your villages - and when I say "your villages," I'm referring to Jagodnja and Joseva - was anyone killed in these artillery attacks?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two civilians, elderly people; Sacir Ibrahimovic and Sahiba Habic. They were around 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was there at some stage an infantry attack on your villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there one later? And please tell us what month we're in.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: May 1992. That is to say after six or seven days, I can't remember exactly, the shelling started up all over again at Joseva and then the infantry attacks followed from the direction of Fakovici, Radijevici, Boljevici, Zlijebac, and Bijeli Kamen. And there was a fierce attack, I mean all available weaponry was being used, and I was at Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was going to ask you. Where did you observe this from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: When the actual shelling of the village of Joseva started, together with a group of people, perhaps four or five of them, I climbed up to a place from where you could see the area of Joseva - the place is called Bradva [phoen] - and there was a thicket there, and we were hiding there. And in the course of that infantry attack, we noticed Serb soldiers coming from Jezero, that is to say the same direction as Fakovici, and with the naked eye we could actually recognise some of them, and we could hear their orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm going to take it one step at a time. Firstly, this place called Jezero, how far is that from Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It is -- well, look, it's a hill. And you have to understand that Jagodnja is in a hilly area. So it is a pass kind of thing, and there was a small lake there. And right below there are fields and then the houses. So, it was 3, 4, 500 metres. I can't really be precise there, but it's fairly close.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just to distinguish it. We're familiar with another Jezero, Your Honours, and just to make clear that's a different Jezero.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned what you could see with the naked eye. Now, did you just have the naked eye or were you using these improvised or hunting binoculars that day in your group of three or four people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We had the hunting binoculars, that is to say my neighbour, who was a hunter, had those binoculars, and he was present there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you mentioned "Serb soldiers coming from Jezero, that is to say the same direction from Fakovici," I'm quoting from the transcript. Were these soldiers in uniforms or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Almost all of them were wearing uniforms, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how many of them were there, approximately? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately -- between 50 and a hundred, as far as we could see with the naked eye. It stretched from above the village of Joseva where there is forest, and then the pass, and then the field. And as they were coming out of the woods, they dispersed and we could hear their orders from their commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you've started describing this you've described how infantry came from different directions. You've been describing these soldiers coming from Fakovici. Are these 50 to 100 people coming from Fakovici or are they coming from all around?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Those people were coming from that direction, from Fakovici. I don't know whether there were any people from Radijevici, I don't know, but they came from that direction, as I said. And the others were coming from the other side, from Zlijebac, Bijeli Kamen, and Godzevici, descending from that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the transcript isn't entirely clear, so I want to make this absolutely clear: The 50 to 100 people, were they coming from Fakovici or were they coming from other places?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: These 50 to 100 people were coming directly from Fakovici and that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Fine. And then for the other people --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I'm happy that the witness has been able to offer the testimony, but I believe that Defence counsel before said that -- asked the question and the response that he got was that they were coming from Jezero, the direction of Fakovici. So could we just clarify now exactly are we changing that testimony or are we trying to refine it, so that we can understand, as Defence counsel would want us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it can be addressed very simply. I do understand your point, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I say one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The moment we establish where Zlijebac, Bijeli Kamen, Godzevici, and the other places, and Radijevici, we know where it is. The moment we establish where those other places are, more or less we can see whether the witness is just confirming what he said earlier or whether he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, he certainly isn't changing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would imagine so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to make clear, Your Honour, the transcript, there was an ambiguity in the answer. The answer was clear: "These people were coming from that direction, from Fakovici. I don't know whether there were any people from Radijevici ..." is a separate phrase, so it was very important for me simply to clarify that ambiguity, and that's what I was trying to achieve, because otherwise one might read, "I don't know whether they were coming from Fakovici." It's very important so I'm going to approach it very carefully, step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: First of all, you have said that these 50 to 100 people were coming from Fakovici. You also mentioned Jezero. Can you tell us why you say that the people were coming from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because Judge Eser has got a small problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps it would help if you ask first the witness to mark on the map more or less where he believes this Jezero is in the vicinity of Jagodnja and that should solve -- you should solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you would, please, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then of course, Mr. Jones, you go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And could you kindly put that X in a square, please. Could you put that X in a square. Put a square around it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And so -- can you write "Jezero" next to it, "Jezero."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Alic. And I thank you, Mr. Jones, for being patient with us. Perhaps you can proceed now with -- and my apologies to you for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour, I do want this evidence to be crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'm going back to the very first answer you gave, and you said "In the course of that infantry attack, we noticed Serb soldiers coming from Jezero, that is to say the same direction from Fakovici." That was the first answer the witness said, so there's to be no doubt that that's what he said. Please explain to us why you say that soldiers coming from Jezero is the direction of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: These soldiers who were coming -- I mean, I said they were coming from Fakovici because there was no other place they could have possibly come from. Soldiers could only have come to that place from Fakovici. It wasn't possible for soldiers to come from anywhere else but just from the direction of Fakovici because that place was above Fakovici and we knew full well that they could only have come from there. And I also recognise some of the soldiers from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, tell us now who you recognised from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I recognised Djoko Djokic and Slavko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And I am going to come back to those people, but still, just in terms of the numbers of soldiers who attacked you, your village. You've said that it was the soldiers coming from the direction of Fakovici, but you also earlier mentioned soldiers coming from a bunch of other locations on the other side. I can check the transcript -- in fact, I'll do that. Yes. You said: "And the others were coming from the other side, Zlijebac, Bijeli Kamen and Godzevici."

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So how many soldiers were coming from those directions? How many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Not from those directions. We were focussing on that group only, I myself did. But from those directions, they were entering the village of Jaseva from below and there was a considerable presence of those soldiers. I mean, including the village Bradici, Caklovici, and Jaketici, and all villages were entering Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think the transcript is quite clear. What the witness said in fact when he said not from these directions, he said: I wasn't focussing on those directions, and it doesn't seem to have made it into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Perhaps he can repeat himself what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Alic, by Mr. Jones to state how many soldiers were coming from those directions, that's Zlijebac, Bijeli Kamen, and the other place, I forgot what the name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Godzevici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Godzevici. What was your answer? What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I answered that. I wasn't in a position to see from where I was how many soldiers were coming from that direction. They were entering the village from below Joseva, and I'm talking about the soldiers coming from that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- clear enough? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that you recognised Slavko Jovanovic and Djoko Djokic. They were from where?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you know Djoko Djokic before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a student at the primary school of Fakovici, Djoko Djokic was the teacher. He used to teach physics and mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how often did you see him when you were a student at the primary school and he was a teacher?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, on every working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And over how many years?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Four years. Plus when I went to school in Bratunac as well because every Sunday I -- or rather, every week on Friday I would travel through Fakovici where I would get off, and that's where I used to see him. So for three years throughout the time that I was attending school at Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How familiar were you with his physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I knew him very well because he used to be my teacher. And he used to wear a beard very often and I could recognise him easily on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you familiar with his voice?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was familiar with his voice and his gait, the manner in which he moved in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If Your Honours would give me one moment. I'm afraid I can't find it at the moment in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But tell us what precisely you saw and heard when you saw Djoko Djokic and Slavko Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that general panic on our part, because we were rather frightened, I mean there was this considerable shooting, we spotted the soldiers as they were coming out of the forest and moving in the direction of Joseva, and I recognised those men, the ones I've mentioned. And I could hear Slavko Jovanovic issuing orders, and he was telling them to enter the village of Joseva. And we were putting up no resistance at all. Our fighters were not present in Joseva, or any other group that could have put up any resistance, so they entered the village. And the order was to set everything on fire and to kill as many as they could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am really sorry I keep interrupting, but for the second time the witness has said something. He said that the order was for them to start shooting, and he had said it before. And it has not mentioned -- and this has not been mentioned in the transcript. So it was the way the fighters were supposed to enter the village, the formation, the military formation, aimed at shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you confirm that, Mr. Alic, that that is exactly what you said before? I'm only asking you because Ms. Vidovic is suggesting that some of the things that you stated did not show up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, in the beginning when I first started recounting this story, I said that they were ordered to get organised in a military formation in order to arrive at firing positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. Let me do it myself. Did you effectively hear any orders to shoot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I heard the orders, and that's what I was trying to explain, the way this order was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can leave it at that now. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way in which these soldiers were presented was important. It said they were deployed in a firing position; it's not a military formation, it is a firing position. So the interpreters are not doing a proper job, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That has been entered into the record now. So it is important, yes, of course, I recognise that. Let's continue, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One matter. You said that - it's off the screen now - "our fighters were not in Joseva." Can you explain what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The hunting rifles that were left behind -- I mean, the people collected those hunting rifles and fled the village and they put up no resistance whatsoever. And not a single person fired a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you actually have a group of fighters in Joseva at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned what you heard Slavko Jovanovic saying. Did you hear Djoko Djokic saying anything?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Djoko Djokic kept repeating for them to continue towards Joseva and to set fire on everything they could possibly set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who was he saying that to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: He was saying this to the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And did -- did the Serb soldiers in fact carry out the orders to shoot and set fire to buildings?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you actually see with your own eyes the Serbs actually shooting people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Describe for us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: From where we were, the place called Bradva, that is we could see immediately they came out of the woods and they entered the village itself and the torching of houses started off straight away, the killing of cattle. And from where I was standing, one can see with the naked eye a group of civilians who were crossing a crossroads at the centre of the village. There were women and two children there, and they approached those soldiers very calmly. And all of a sudden we heard shots being fired by the soldiers. And so they mowed them all down, all of the people who happened to be there, at close range.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know the family -- or do you know the names of the women and two children who were shot, mowed down?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the names of the children exactly. It was a family called Paraganlija. There was a mother-in-law with her two daughters-in-law and their two children, and according to other neighbours and a man from one of these families, the two women, the two daughters-in-law were actually pregnant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And at what range did they get shot, how close?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was so close, perhaps 10 metres, because afterwards the neighbours told us that those women worked for Serbs in the surrounding villages, Bradici and Zlijebac, and they thought that they wouldn't be killed and that's why they approached these soldiers quite calmly. But in spite of that, an indescribable event took place that is simply very hard to describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you have described how you were focussing on a group of soldiers who came from Jezero from the direction of Fakovici. The soldiers who shot these pregnant women and the children, were they from that group, from Fakovici, or from some other group?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. The people who came from the upper side and from the lower side of the village, it encompassed the other hamlets of Joseva, Mesanovici, just before Joseva. But I can't actually confirm specifically at the moment. It was possible that others were involved, but 90 per cent it was people who had come from the direction of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And you've mentioned that you heard Djoko Djokic telling soldiers to move on, to burn and to kill. And you've mentioned Slavko Jovanovic giving orders. These soldiers, do you know whether they were in Djoko Djokic's group or in Slavko Jovanovic's group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour, I haven't heard any testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't heard any testimony about groups of the two, and unless there is testimony that the two men had two groups and that can be clarified, I think it would be difficult for Mr. Alic to understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I think you would need to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let's start with Slavko Jovanovic. You said: "And I could hear Slavko Jovanovic issuing orders and he was telling them to enter the village of Joseva." Now, who was he issuing orders to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: To the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Go ahead, Mr. Alic, that's what you are here for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said I saw Slavko Jovanovic and Djoko Djokic who arrived from one direction, but I said nothing about the two groups. I talked about this one direction and about them deploying themselves in a firing position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That confirms exactly the validity of Ms. Sellers' objection. I think you need to address it -- address it in whichever way you want. I think you can even put direct questions in this regard. It's not going to do any harm. Provided we do have a clarification, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So Slavko Jovanovic was issuing orders to Serb soldiers. Was he some kind of a commander, as far as you could tell, in this action?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: According to the orders he gave, yes, that appeared to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And does the same apply to Djoko Djokic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, they were in the same group, so probably Djoko Djokic was a commander of sorts, too. Whether a minor group or a major group is not something that I know. I wouldn't venture into that because I wasn't there where they were giving orders directly, telling people what to do, but they were both telling soldiers what to do and issuing them with instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So dealing with that - and you've used the word "group" now, they were in the same group, Djoko Djokic and Slavko Jovanovic - my question was: The killings of the Paraganlija family, was that done by this group of soldiers who were being issued commands by Djoko Djokic and Slavko Jovanovic or was it by some other people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The group that I've described, the group that comprised Slavko Jovanovic and Djoko Djokic, they came from the upper side and entered the village. It was a bit further up from where we were, too far perhaps to say -- to see that it was Slavko Jovanovic of all people, but yes, that group was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That group was where?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Where the civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did they kill those pregnant women because they were afraid of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How would the witness know this??

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's to show the ridiculousness of the idea that the Serbs were massacring people because of fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how does he know --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can ask him to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know why they killed those women? Can you think of any reason?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The reason could have been that they'd been ordered to kill everything that moved and everything they came across in the village itself. So that's why the women were killed, quite literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right, because they'd been ordered to kill. Now, how many houses were burned in Joseva that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my estimate, everything burned down that was flammable. There was certain houses that were built concrete that just didn't catch fire, but I would say roughly 90 per cent of the entire village burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: 90 per cent of the village of Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did this attack affect the people in Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The attack horrified all those who were in Joseva who had fled to Jagodnja. There was panic among these people and no one was aware of what the others were doing, how they should go about burying the dead bodies, and there was a person there who was deaf and dumb. At his own threshold he was shot to death and we had to bury his body later on, because part of the body had been burned, incinerated, along with the house. He was lying on the steps, so part of his leg had been burned to a cinder. We buried some of those and those who were just passing through Joseva as well. Livestock were killed, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. So in addition to -- you've mentioned in the Paraganlija family, I think it was the mother-in-law, two pregnant women, two children, you've mentioned this deaf and dumb person, Fehim Dugonjic. Was anyone else killed that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, an elderly man and another younger man who was underage. He was killed in a shed with a bullet through his forehead, but the shed had not been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how did you feel at this stage, the villagers in Jagodnja and Joseva, about the Serbs in Fakovici after this attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to explain the pressure that the people were feeling, the anger and the need to escape. We had to evacuate the entire village of Jagodnja. Our children and our women, we had to move them into the forest in order to set up camp or something like that. We had to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. build makeshift houses - tents, if you like - right there in the middle of the woods in order to prevent the same thing happening that had happened in Joseva, because we expected that Jagodnja itself would be attacked any day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you do anything to give you advance warning of when an attack was going to come?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by "advance warning"? Advance warning to who?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did anyone keep a lookout to see if the Serbs were going to attack again?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. People discussed this, the people who had fled Joseva. They asked to meet in a certain place in Jagodnja, and we had agreed for a group of people to try to put up some sort of resistance to avoid the same thing happening again that had happened at Joseva. So we appointed a person to lead that group. His name was Asim Smajlovic, he was a well-respected person. We organised a small group of people who were then to observe the area around Joseva and Jagodnja in case of a repeated attack, to see whether we could avoid civilians being killed and massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned Asim Smajlovic. What did he do before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Asim Smajlovic was president of the Zlijebac local commune. That's before the war. He was a well-respected citizen, honest, a hard worker. So that's why we appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Were you actually able to dig trenches or anything like that around your villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: It was impossible to have lines established around our village, be it trenches or anything else; it's an enormous area. It would have taken an enormous number of men to cover the area and to cut off all the paths and roads along which Serb soldiers could have come.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how you had, I think it's six or so, hunting rifles. You had been attacked by a large number of Serb soldiers, armed Serb soldiers. If the Serbs came back, what was your plan? Did you have a plan?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: We had no plan at all. We were struck by panic, fear, and anger. We were too listless to be making plans, nor was it our intention to make a plan. It wasn't our intention to resist. This was a mighty force of soldiers, armed to their teeth. We had no intention of resisting. We just believed that observers would be useful to notify the people at Jagodnja in good time so that at least they could escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And where would they escape to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: To the woods. To the woods. There was nowhere else for us to go, just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've described how shelters were made in the woods. Were people having to cook in the woods?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Now, this applies to all the other needs, everything that a family might need, we had to make do with what we had in the woods. We had to go perhaps 1 or 2 kilometres further afield and there was a risk that anyone could be injured or killed, because where we were there was no running water at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You had to go 1 or 2 kilometres to get water I understand from the answer. I don't think it was well interpreted.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it safe to get water from there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you: Nothing was safe any longer in the area that we are talking about. Even the camp in the woods or the civilians there, nobody was safe let alone someone who was going elsewhere to fetch water, to other villages, perhaps. Nothing was safe any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, as far as these lookouts were concerned, people looking out to prevent another massacre, were people ordered to stand as lookouts or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I object to Defence counsel referring to a massacre. We've described five or six killings, and with utmost respect, I think we should keep our terminology in perspective of the testimony of Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. What's your reaction to that, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's an appalling answer. It's certainly a massacre of pregnant women and children. It's not a matter of quantity, it's a matter of the quality of the killing, and I believe this witness has used the expression "massacre," and I'm going to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But apart from the fact that he may have used the word "massacre" himself, I think that one or two persons could be massacred, denoting the way in which they are killed, actually. Let's proceed. Let's not waste or lose time, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It wasn't me who raised this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm suggesting, in other words, to forget looking back into the records to see what the witness said and let's move, because to me, a massacre means also -- is descriptive of the way --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's as I understand it. In any event, to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were people ordered to stand as lookouts to prevent further killings or was it a voluntary activity?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: There were no orders being given in our group. Nobody ordered anyone else to go somewhere and keep a lookout. There were no such orders. Everything was being done on a voluntary basis. Every man who felt that his family was in danger felt the need to go there to watch the area in order to keep his family safe and to keep his family from being killed and massacred, because I am no longer sure myself which expression I should be using.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. We can stick with "killed." Did some people not go on guard?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were those, too, who went elsewhere, to other villages. They were those who didn't have the courage to go out and observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it was possible to refuse to go on guard or to decline to go on guard?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was there another attack by Serbs in our village after this one you've just described?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was an attack on Jagodnja itself. That was in early June, 1992. From the attack against Joseva, there was daily shelling, shells were falling on us, and then the attack ensued. In the early days of June, we were being shelled from the same directions but more from the Fakovici direction. There was chaos among the refugees; they started running into the woods. And there was an infantry attack from the direction of Fakovici, from Zlijebac, and from the direction of Mlecva, meaning now there was more of it coming from the direction of Mlecva and the result was we were surrounded on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was there -- I'm not sure if you've told us precisely that there was -- I have to be very careful now to avoid objections. What sort of -- you've mentioned an infantry attack. So were these Serb soldiers who were attacking the village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did they actually enter Jagodnja on that day?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. On that day Serb soldiers came from the direction of Fakovici and from the direction of Zlijebac and Godzevici, from those general areas and from those villages. They entered one particular part of the village of Bosnjaci, they set fire to it, to the school building, to the mosque, and they came to the hamlet of Tokici, which is part of the village, and started torching it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to take it in parts. You said that the mosque was set fire to. Was that the only damage that was done to --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes what? Because I very much suspect that he answered "yes" to your remark that he had mentioned the burning down of the mosque, but I don't think he had heard the rest of the question as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Aside from the burning, was any other danger done to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The mosque couldn't just burn down in its entirety. There were just parts of the carpet inside the mosque, so it couldn't all just burn down, the entire mosque. So they used hand-held rocket launchers to target the minaret and the roof itself of the old mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did they succeed in damaging the minaret and the roof?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did that mosque pose any danger to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've also mentioned that the school building was set fire to. Is that the one which you mentioned was being used to house refugees?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were those refugees posing any danger to the Serbs and the surrounding villages, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And before this action, had you been attacking, you in Joseva and Jagodnja, had you been attacking the surrounding Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you told us on the first attack when these people were killed, you told us how you didn't resist. On this attack, on this day, did you actually shoot back at the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you personally or was it other people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I had no rifle, but I was there. There were other people who had their hunting rifles and makeshift rifles, too, that we'd made by using water pipes. We had a blacksmith in the village who made those rifles for us. We had three or four such makeshift rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were those makeshift rifles safe to use?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No. Those rifles could have blown up in the face of the shooter as much as those approaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did your -- did the Serbs react to being shot at?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: There was heavy fighting in that part of Hasanovici where Serbs couldn't get in. When shooting started in that part of the area where the Muslims were, as soon as one of the Serbs was wounded or being resisted or perhaps killed, they would, as if by default, withdraw and run back to where they'd come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I think you may partly have answered my next question. Can you explain why the Serbs withdrew when you had so little firepower and they had more?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: As I said, at this time the Serbs were surprised by all the resistance being encountered. When we started firing, I'm referring to those people who had some rifles that they could use, small rifles, the Serbs set fright -- and started to run. They were frightened. What do I know? They had no courage to pursue the path that they had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in other words, they took flight because they were cowards?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They didn't like it if civilians shot back at them.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I certainly see that Mr. Jones has been able to elicit from the witness possibly the reason that the Serbs withdrew or retreated, but I have not heard the witness say that if civilians shot back ... If he wants to clarify that part of his testimony, fine, but it doesn't seem at this point to be what Mr. Alic has said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I think it's the case, Mr. Jones. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: How would you characterise the people who shot at the Serbs? Were they civilians? Were they soldiers? Were they fighters? What word would you use to describe them?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The people firing at those soldiers were civilians. They had no automatic weapons that would have suggested an army. They had no uniform. They had nothing to define them as members of an army. We wore very simple footwear or plastic boots. We had nothing that -- on us that would define us as an army or as soldiers. We didn't look like soldiers. All of the rifles were hunting rifles and makeshift rifles. There was some people who were carrying axes or pitchforks, standing guard, as it were, at their own threshold, prepared to be killed there, but not give away anything that rightfully belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were these people shooting at the Serbs because they had been ordered to shoot at them or were they doing it on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this again: No one ordered anyone else to shoot. It wasn't possible for anyone to stop someone right there in the middle of the village and tell them to shoot at someone unless they wanted to. I mean shooting at the Serb soldiers who came in to burn our village down, or what remained of it, what little remained of it. No one was in a position to order anyone else to shoot at someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just one matter which I think you mentioned in relation to the first attack on Joseva. You mentioned cattle, that you had cattle. What happened to the cattle on the first attack and what, if anything, happened to the cattle on this attack?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: During this attack, Serbs, as they were retreating from the area, came across cattle in sheds. They would burn down the sheds, and then the cattle would die, too. This was a very serious thing, and it was a disaster. They found some cattle outside around the meadows, too, and they would kill them. And there was almost an epidemic, so the cattle had to be buried as well as the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know why they were shooting your cattle?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what my conclusion was. They were shooting cattle so that we could no longer survive in the area, so that we would have to go elsewhere for our livelihood. Cattle is a fundamental necessity in the area that I come from. You have to milk cows in order to have milk. You need milk in order to feed your children. You need it for sustenance [Realtime transcript read in error "substance"], and that's why the Serb soldiers destroyed everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. And it was "sustenance," I think we'll all agree, in the last sentence. Did any vehicles come to Jagodnja that day, and I'm talking about the later attack in June?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Following the withdrawal of the Serb units and army, they went back to where they'd come from. Shortly after, there was a vehicle coming from Joseva, and this was the only road that was still fit for travel. The vehicle could only have come from Joseva, not from Fakovici. This was a Niva vehicle with a red cross on its doors. This vehicle reached the centre of the village of Trkici that had been torched. We happened to be there. We were trying to salvage whatever we could from the houses in terms of clothes, food, blankets, to keep the whole lot from burning down, because we needed these things. The vehicle arrived and a single shot was fired at this vehicle. The vehicle, as if by default, crashed into a fence --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just stop you there just to break the answer up. We'll have the break, so just one question: Who, if anyone, eventually came out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: There were two soldiers in the vehicle, two soldiers wearing uniform. Out of experience, we knew we shouldn't come too close to that vehicle, so we took cover behind the houses and then the soldiers escaped from the vehicle. We came closer, perhaps 10 or 15 minutes later, to the vehicle and found in it a considerable quantity of ammunition, a whole crate of automatic weapon ammunition; two automatic rifles; two shells, two mortar shells; one Zolja; a whole crate full of bombs or grenades. The best thing that we found was medicines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's an appropriate moment to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Jones. We'll have a 25-minute break, that's -- we'll start again at quarter past 6.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, before the break you had been describing this vehicle, this Niva, and you said: "Out of experience we knew we shouldn't come too close to that vehicle." Can you explain what you meant by that,

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: What I meant was in order to avoid shooting from the vehicle and the people to be injured or wounded or, God forbid, even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've mentioned that this car, that it had a Red Cross symbol. You also described how Serb soldiers came out of it and it had weapons and ammunition which you found in it. Did you personally find those items? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I was there. I was there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Next to the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to the items you found in the car in a moment. Did you find anything else in the area from where Serbs had been shooting that day in Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Apart from the things I've already mentioned, medicines and sanitary equipment, we saw a place slightly away from that vehicle from where the Serb soldiers were shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In the backpack that we found there, there was food and a first aid kit. And there was a document there which said "Bajida" [phoen] and a number of names of Serb soldiers, in my view, because it was mostly names of the soldiers from that area, the surrounding villages of Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Any village which you have in mind specifically or which was referred to in the document?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: This Bajida person was from Zlijebac and there was a list of people from Zlijebac, and I myself knew Bajida personally because he was a bus driver employed by the company called Vihor in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to these documents which were found?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were thrown into the rubbish because it didn't mean anything to us. There was nobody that we could have given them to or submitted them to or anything of the sort. It meant nothing to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's get this clear because it's a little bit confused in my mind. Bajida is the name of a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a nickname of a person from Zlijebac. That was what he was called, and I don't know his actual real name and surname. But on the basis of this nickname, I recognise that this is a person from Zlijebac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I ask Defence counsel -- the witness's testimony again is slightly unclear. Mr. Alic referred to a document with Bajida, the name, and then later on I see that the question pertains to documents. Are we talking about a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Document, I think it may be a problem of interpretation. I take it that we're talking of this just one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I can clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was it a single document or more than one document, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a single document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What does "Bajida" mean in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Bajida" is some kind of nickname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But what does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Does it mean anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it -- yeah, what does it mean, first of all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That person nicknamed Bajida was called by that name before the war; that's how I knew him, by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think it means anything in Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it doesn't mean anything, it doesn't mean anything. I was just trying to see whether it had any connotation at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's -- it is definitely an Arabic word. So I just wanted to see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps it means something in Maltese.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not a Maltese, it is an Arabic word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned how in this car, the Niva, documentation was found, but you also said how important medicines were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one clarification. You're quite right. This word "Bajida" would appear to be Arabic, and the witness has said it in another way, "Baida" [phoen], which is a Serb word. The interpreters, unfortunately, can't hear the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. One is "Baida" and the other one is "Bajida."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So going back to these medicines. As a result of finding the medicines in that car, did that -- did that make any -- as a result of that, did you in fact take on a new career, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since the medicines and bandages were found, and a bag which was full of those medicines, my neighbours told me that we should appoint Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. somebody who should take care of these things. Since we had no doctors or nurses in our midst or anyone else who might have been an expert on those matters, I myself decided and I was told by my elders that I could be the appointed person. And so it was decided that I would be the person in charge of these matters in future in case there was any need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how would you describe that role which you took on?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I can describe the role quite simply. I mean, whenever I saw something -- and I mean, I never knew anything much about medicines or anything like that, but I had a cousin who was a nurse and she was from Osmace. And so I had to go see her at Osmace. I had to seek her out. And it was by pure chance that I actually managed to find her, and she explained to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: -- everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to break this down, and if you can give shorter answers so we can make progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'm also trusting that, this not being a very contentious issue, that I can lead to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Basically, did you become a nurse? Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in order to know what to do, you told us that you had a cousin who was a nurse and she was from Osmace and you went to seek her out. Was he actually in Osmace itself or in the hamlet of Osmace?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was in a hamlet of Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: What's the name of that hamlet?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: The hamlet is called Murselovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, did you go there, find her, and as you said, by chance, receive some sort of instruction and then return to your village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: I went there and I found her and she gave me all the instructions. Yes, I went there by chance, but I had to go there. I had to find somebody who could give me some indication of what I was supposed to do, to instruct me in some way so I could do it in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that an easy trip to make to Murselovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Because above the village of Jagodnja where we tried to pass, there could have been killings and all sorts of things there because it's a forest. And Osmace is 25 kilometres away, approximately, so we went through the creeks. We made our way through the forests and creeks all the way to Osmace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the hamlet does appear on the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- but to save time, I wouldn't propose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I have marked it already on my map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say "we" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's mountainous terrain and forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say "we," who went with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were two other lads who helped me carry all the stuff. And for security reasons as well, because we were travelling through the woods, as I said. We were deep in the forest and we were afraid. We feared for our lives, and there could have an ambush at any moment, all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to move forward to once you returned to your village. And just so you can give us a sense of life over the summer of 1992, firstly, did you continue to receive refugees, Muslim refugees, who had been expelled by Serbs from their villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Up until the first attack from Joseva, or rather in Joseva, which happened in mid-May, all the surrounding Muslim villages around Jagodnja, the ones that I've marked, that is to say Skelani, Tihici, Daljegosta, Abdulici, all those people had already arrived into our villages, so there were no Muslims that could have arrived from that area. Not a single Muslim was left in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you -- sorry, in what area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you say Skelani, Tihici, Daljegosta, what area is that that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: That's the area of the municipality of Skelani. So from that part of the area, Muslims had all been chased out of there until mid-May 1992. From there and from Abdulici and thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever receive refugees in your village from further afield, from different municipalities altogether; not from Bratunac, Srebrenica, Skelani, but even other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Afterwards in June, July, refugees started arriving, looking for food. People from Visegrad, from Zepa, from Rogatica, from Han Pijesak, refugees driven out of that area were crossing the woods. It was, so to say, a no-man's land. Nobody on the Muslim side was in control and Serbs or Serb patrols might have been there near Jagodnja and Joseva. And they were making their way through the woods, looking for food, coming to us for food, in June and July. People from Joseva -- I mean, the village had been torched and there was just a part of the village called Hasanici which was left standing. And all those people went back to where they had come from in order to gather some food for sheer survival, in order to get to their crops or see if there was anything left over in terms of cattle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say these people went back to where they'd come from in order to gather some food, is there anywhere specific you have in mind, any villages?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: People who were from the village of Abdulici or Zanjevo, rather, were trying to go down there in order to get some food. They would step on mines, they would end up in minefields or be ambushed or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask if the witness could be shown D42, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you'll see that this is a document dated 10th, September, 1996, of the 314th Infantry Brigade command. And it's recommendation concerning Radivoje Jakovljevic. And I'll just read the explanation because it's quite short. "Radivoje Jakovljevic has been -- or was been a member of the VRS, Republika Srpska army, since military operations began. He participated in fighting in the Fakovici neighbourhood sector. He displayed steadiness and bravery in all situations and enjoyed the respect of the soldiers and the people for that reason. When reconnoitring the terrain on 15th August, 1992, he was seriously wounded (by stepping on a mine) in Radijevici village, and died in hospital the same day from injuries received." Now, I want to ask you first to look at the map. I believe you've marked Radijevici already. Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've also marked Boljevici, which is where this Radivoje Jakovljevic was apparently born in 1933. So according to this document he would have been 59 years old when he died. Now, is Boljevici, is that part of Fakovici local commune?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And according to this document, this gentleman was a member of the Republika Srpska army since military operations began and before his death on 15 August 1992, according to this, he "participated in fighting in the Fakovici neighbourhood sector." Now, can you confirm that there was indeed fighting in the Fakovici neighbourhood sector before 15th August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps I put it badly. Let me put it this way: Your village is in the neighbourhood of Fakovici, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, our village is in the vicinity of Fakovici, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. And you've told us about the units coming from the direction of Fakovici into your village in June 1992. Now, if someone living in Fakovici, a Serb, would say that all was peaceful in that area until October of 1992, would that be true?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify that, please. What part do you mean? Where was it peaceful?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me approach it a different way. This refers to a person being killed stepping on a mine in Radijevici. Were you aware that Serbs had laid mines in Radijevici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that Serbs had laid minefields in this area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the people from Zanjevo who were looking for food had left and that after the attack at Jagodnja in the beginning of July, they used to go down there and they would come across minefields. And they tried to go around them, and some people were killed. And on the basis of their experiences, we did know that they -- there were land-mines in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, that's land-mines in or around Zanjevo. Were there other -- were there ever minefields closer to your village, to Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the geographical position itself, the way the village is organised and the fact that it is surrounded by forests and the way the Serb soldiers approached the village, they were known to lay land-mines next to our fields. They would come through the woods at night, and when they were on patrol, they would leave land-mines. And so if Muslims did any reconnaissance or try to go to the forests for any other purpose, they would be likely to step on mines. And this was at the end of June, the beginning of July; those things happened at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've mentioned how the Serbs laid land-mines next to your fields. The Prosecution may suggest to you that the laying of land-mines is a defensive use of those weapons. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Will you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: Did those minefields in fact make it difficult for you to move around your area, you Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. People would go to Zanjevo on a daily basis to forage for food. They had no food. We didn't have food ourselves at Jagodnja and Joseva, those of us who survived in the area, let alone those who had been expelled from the area. They had already eaten up all the food that we had.
