utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's clear. Now, did you at any stage see any indications or markings or signposts indicating where mines had been laid?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Where did you see those signposts or markings or indications?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: As for the markings, some of the mines were laid near Joseva from the direction of Fakovici and Radijevici. On your way there you would find signposts reading "Watch out, mines." But they were placed in the direction that the Serb soldiers were coming from, not in our direction. But the road that the Serb soldiers were taking, those were wooden signposts driven into the ground, and this is what they said in order to keep the Serb soldiers from stepping on any of those mines that they were unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you've mentioned Osmace earlier in your testimony. During the summer of 1992, did you in Jagodnja and Joseva have any sort of regular contact with Osmace?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know a place called Kragljivoda?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in the summer of 1992, did you in Jagodnja and Joseva have regular contact with Kragljivoda?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did some people nonetheless manage to occasionally go back and forth between these places?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Those people who were moving about, for the most part people who had families in that area, they would go see their families and then go back. People went to look for food and then would bring it back. They would stay several days in Jagodnja until they were given some food or in order to use an opportunity to join someone on their way to Zanjevo to get food, if the people from Zanjevo happened to be moving in that direction, because they were familiar with the road or the path leading there. So those were the lines of communication that people were using, those people who were in fact moving about the area. But the fear was great and they regularly took round-about routes because it wasn't possible to just cross the elevation in order to reach those areas directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, moving to a slightly different topic. You've described how Joseva was burnt in May 1992. During the summer of 1992, did those houses which had been burned remain empty or did people try to rebuild them?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Most of the people whose houses had been burned tried to go back and did in fact go back to the village -- to the village of Joseva. They would use the two walls where there was no roof in order to make shelters that they could live in and in order to get there in time for the crop that they had sown the previous spring, corn and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did the Serbs in your area notice that people were moving back into Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. You could see that with the naked eye. From Bijeli Kamen you could see all of it happening. They were active on a daily basis, firing on both Joseva and Jagodnja. People who were working the fields, the wheat had been planted in autumn 1999 [as interpreted], and in August it was already ripe for picking, for harvesting. And there was a lot to be done on the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think there might be an error with the date. Did you say autumn 1999 or some other year?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In autumn, that's when wheat is planted. That was in 1991. I may have made a mistake myself, which I apologise for, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And then you mentioned that because of -- there was harvest and a lot of work to be done, you've linked that to the fact that there was -- let me just get this right. To the fact that they were active on a daily basis, firing on both Joseva and Jagodnja. So who are you referring to there as being active on a daily basis, firing on both Joseva and Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did they do anything with regard to any wheat which was harvested, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In late August they succeeded in harvesting some of the wheat at night in order to tie the wheat up into bales, as we used to call them. We couldn't work the fields by using our machinery because there was no fuel, and the women tried to harvest as much as they could, pick up as much as they could, to make bread. We were waiting for another window of opportunity to go there and harvest the wheat. We threshed the wheat with our spades in order to be able to harvest some of it to make bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But my question is with regard to the Serbs. Did the Serbs do anything with regard to the wheat that was harvested?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: They were shelling us daily. We couldn't get to the fields to work the fields by day or by night. In late September, possibly early October, the Serbs used incendiary ammunition to set fire to the stacks of hay that were on the fields, wounding civilians as a result and killing cattle, whatever cattle was still moving. They used every opportunity to strike fear into us, to try to drive us away or to kill us and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. You've taken us up to late September, possibly early October now. Do you recall any other events in early October 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: In early October 1992, there were fierce attacks, heavy shelling, incursions by Serb soldiers, a group of Serb soldiers -- groups of Serb soldiers into both Jagodnja and Joseva. They intimidated the civilians there. They were shooting. They were trying to kill someone or take people away. This became our daily tragedy. There wasn't a single moment of time for us to perform any of our daily tasks. As a nurse, I was in Jagodnja at the house in Hasanovici. Every day there was somebody who was wounded who needed seeing to. I was so busy that I was no longer able to keep an eye on what was going on in the fields nearby. I dressed their wounds, I suffered together with these wounded people. It was dreadful and I would probably need a lot of time to explain everything that was going on in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's sufficient for our purposes for the time being. Did you always remain in Jagodnja or did you ever go outside your village in the course of these attacks? And I'm referring to early October 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC
utterances.text: Personally I was at Jagodnja throughout. I never left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm trying to recall, Your Honour, are we going until 7.00 or 6.45?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever is -- the time when we are supposed to stop is 7.00, but I am noticing some tiredness on the part of the witness in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I might just ask a couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead. Provided you don't exceed 7.00. And I don't know what Ms. Sellers --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to inform the Trial Chamber and the Defence also that we would like to make a very short submission prior to the close of today, possibly after the witness has already withdrawn from the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suppose, what I suggest, Mr. Jones, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can dispose of the witness. He can be escorted out of the courtroom. Mr. Alic, we are going to stop here because we've got some other business to transact today before we go home. You will return again tomorrow in the afternoon, like today. We start at quarter past 2.00. In the meantime, between today and tomorrow and in the days to come, between sittings you are not to contact anyone or allow anyone to contact you to discuss or mention matters related to your testimony or to the events that you are giving testimony about. Did I make myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't mean to say that you cannot ring up your family, for example, to put their mind at rest that you are okay, but you are not to discuss matters related to the events that we are dealing with. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll see you again tomorrow afternoon then. Usher, you can escort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, earlier today, prior to Mr. Alic commencing his testimony, the Defence informed the Trial Chamber and also the Prosecution at the same time that Dr. Ilijaz Pilav would not be coming to testify, and the Defence stated that it was in the interest of not having redundancy of the testimony offered before the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution would like to put on the record that we prepared quite a bit for Mr. -- Dr. Pilav. We thought he was an important witness, and we thought that he was going to go into many others that we weren't redundant, and we just would like to state that any type of prior notification, particularly with a doctor whose schedule is probably known more than two or three days in advance, would have been appreciated by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. So we can adjourn -- yes, Madam Vidovic. Can't you leave it at that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, at any rate we ourselves were notified quite late in the day. I do have to say I'm glad that Ms. Sellers said this. We also some time ago were preparing for Dr. Pilav who was on the Prosecution list. We had put together our own questions for him and they struck the witness from the list. At any rate, had we known earlier, we would have duly notified the OTP. We were trying to make our call until very late in the day, whether we would be calling this witness at a later stage or not. But it was after the testimony of Dr. Mardel that we surveyed some other circumstances and decided that his testimony would likely be redundant. I don't think, therefore, that there is any particular sense in making an objection like this, since the witness was originally on their own list and they were the ones who gave up on calling that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You definitely, Ms. Vidovic, have the right to withdraw a witness if you want to, just as the Prosecution has a right to do that. And there is nothing either side can do; it's a prerogative that you have. The only thing is that -- anyway, let me say the least possible because in this case it seems that this was a witness that both of you wanted to bring forward. We can adjourn now. I thank you all, and we'll meet again tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of October, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
